title: Amber, Electric Fish and Rubbing Machines
summary: Rub a piece of golden amber with fur and it can pick up bits of straw like magic. For two thousand years people wondered why. Then curious scientists built spinning balls that made sparks and sent electricity racing along a thread.

sections.heading: The Golden Stone That Grabbed Straw
paragraphs: Pick up a piece of amber and it feels surprisingly warm and light for a stone. That is because it is not really a stone at all. Amber is fossilised tree resin, the sticky, sweet-smelling goo that oozes out of a pine tree when its bark is damaged. Millions of years ago, blobs of resin dripped down ancient trees, sometimes trapping insects, spiders or tiny leaves. Buried under layers of sand and mud, squeezed and warmed for ages, the resin slowly hardened into amber. Some pieces are around 100 million years old, from the time of the dinosaurs.

The most famous amber in Europe comes from the shores of the Baltic Sea. Storms wash it up on the beaches of what are now Poland, Lithuania and the Russian region of Kaliningrad, where about 90 percent of the world's minable amber lies. Since prehistoric times people have collected these honey-coloured lumps and traded them far to the south along routes that historians call the Amber Road. By Roman times, Baltic amber was being carried all the way to the Mediterranean, where it was carved into beads, charms and jewellery.

Somewhere along the way, people noticed something odd. If you polish or rub a piece of amber with a dry cloth or a scrap of fur, it starts to attract light things. Bits of straw, dry leaves, feathers and dust jump up and cling to it. Rub it hard enough in very dry air and you might even hear a tiny crackle or see a faint spark in the dark. To an ancient jeweller or merchant this must have seemed magical. A stone that reaches out and grabs things, without touching them!

You can try a modern version yourself. Rub a plastic comb or balloon on a woollen jumper or your hair, then hold it near some tiny pieces of tissue paper. They leap up and stick. That pull is exactly what ancient people saw with amber. Today we call it static electricity: electric charge that builds up on a surface and stays there until it leaks away or jumps off as a spark. But it would take more than two thousand years for anyone to work out what was really going on.

Here is a puzzle that took a very long time to solve. The straw or tissue paper is not charged at all, so why should it be pulled toward the amber? The answer is that a charged object nudges the tiny charges inside nearby things. When negatively charged amber comes close to a scrap of straw, it pushes some of the straw's negative charges slightly away to the far side, leaving the near side a little positive. Because opposite charges attract and the near side is closer, the pull wins over the push, and up jumps the straw. The same trick lets a rubbed balloon cling to a wall.

sections.heading: Thales: Tradition, Not Proof
paragraphs: If you look up who discovered static electricity, many books give a confident answer: Thales of Miletus, around 600 BCE. Thales was a real person, a Greek thinker who lived in Miletus, a busy trading city on the coast of what is now Turkey. Later Greeks counted him as one of the Seven Sages, the wise men of early Greece, and many historians call him one of the first philosophers, because he tried to explain the world through nature rather than through stories about gods.

But here is the problem. Not a single word that Thales himself wrote has survived. Everything we know about him comes from people writing much later. The philosopher Aristotle, writing around two hundred years after Thales, reported that Thales thought a magnet, the natural magnetic stone called lodestone, must have a kind of soul, because it could move iron. Much of the rest of Thales's story comes from a writer named Diogenes Laërtius, who lived about eight hundred years after Thales and sometimes repeated unreliable tales.

The link between Thales and amber is a tradition that grew up in these later writings. It may contain a grain of truth, since Greek thinkers clearly did know that rubbed amber attracts small things. But we cannot say for certain that Thales was the first to notice it, or that he did any experiments with it at all. It is a bit like the famous story that Thales predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE, which comes from the historian Herodotus and which many modern historians doubt.

So the fair way to say it is this: according to tradition, Thales of Miletus noticed that amber rubbed with fur attracts light objects. Probably many ordinary people noticed it long before any philosopher wrote about it. What the Greeks did give us for certain is the name. Their word for amber was elektron. Some scholars link it to an old Greek word for the shining Sun, perhaps because of amber's warm, golden glow, and in one Greek myth amber was formed from the tears of grieving sisters of Phaethon, the boy who crashed the chariot of the Sun.

Two thousand years later, that ancient word for a golden stone would become the root of the words electric, electricity, electron and electronics. Every time you charge a phone, you are using a word that began as the Greek name for fossil tree resin.

sections.heading: Fish That Fight with Lightning
paragraphs: Long before anyone used the word electricity, people had felt its sting in a very different way: from fish. Certain fish can make their own electric shocks, and fishermen around the world learned to respect them.

In ancient Egypt, the Nile catfish could give a painful jolt. Egyptian texts from around 2750 BCE refer to a fish they called the thunderer of the Nile. In the Mediterranean, Greeks and Romans knew the electric ray, a flat, round fish that lies half-buried in the sand on the sea floor, waiting for small fish to swim by. When prey comes close, the ray zaps it. Depending on the species, electric rays can produce shocks of about 8 to 220 volts. Touch one by accident and your hand and arm go numb. The Romans called this fish torpedo, from a Latin verb meaning to be stiffened or paralysed. (Much later, the underwater weapon was named after the fish.)

The numbing power of the torpedo was so well known that the Greek philosopher Plato used it as a joke. In his dialogue called the Meno, a young man complains that talking to the famous thinker Socrates leaves his mind as numb as if he had been stung by a torpedo fish.

Some ancient doctors tried to put the shocks to use. The Roman physician Scribonius Largus worked at the court of the emperor Claudius. Around 46 to 47 CE he collected 271 medical recipes into a book called Compositiones. One of them was unusual. For a bad headache, he advised placing a live torpedo fish on the painful spot until the numbness took the pain away. For gout, a painful swelling of the joints, the patient was told to stand at the seashore with a living electric fish under their foot. Scribonius Largus did not know anything about electricity, but today he is sometimes mentioned as an early example of using electrical stimulation of nerves to treat pain, an idea that modern medicine really does use in some devices.

How can a fish make electricity? Electric fish have special organs made of stacks of flat cells called electrocytes. When a nerve signal reaches them, tiny charged particles called ions rush through the cell walls, making one side of each cell slightly positive and the other slightly negative. Each cell gives only a small voltage, but thousands of them stacked in a row add up, just like batteries placed end to end in a torch. The champion is the electric eel of South America: one species can produce up to about 860 volts.

For a very long time, nobody connected these shocking fish with the attraction of rubbed amber. One was a strange animal power and the other a curiosity of a jewel. Only in the 1700s did scientists show that the fish shocks were electrical, and, as we will see in a later part, the stacked cells of electric fish even helped inspire the first battery.

sections.heading: Dr Gilbert and His Little Earth
paragraphs: For about two thousand years after the Greeks, people knew that rubbed amber attracted straw and that lodestone attracted iron, and most of them assumed these were two versions of the same mysterious pull. The man who finally untangled them was an English doctor named William Gilbert.

Gilbert was born around 1544 in Colchester, in Essex, and studied at St John's College, Cambridge, becoming a doctor of medicine in 1569. He moved to London, built a successful medical practice and rose to become president of the Royal College of Physicians in 1600. From 1601 he served as one of the personal physicians of Queen Elizabeth I. But his great passion was magnets, and he spent years testing them.

In 1600 he published his findings in a book written in Latin, the international language of scholars. Its short title is De Magnete, meaning On the Magnet. What made the book special was its method. Gilbert did not just repeat what ancient authors had said. He did experiments, again and again, and he scoffed at writers who copied old stories without testing them. Today he is often counted among the first true experimental scientists in England.

One of his most famous experiments used a terrella, Latin for little Earth: a ball carved out of lodestone. Gilbert moved a small compass needle around the ball and found that it behaved just like a compass on the real Earth, pointing toward the poles and tipping downward more and more as it got closer to them. From this he made a bold claim: the whole Earth is a giant magnet. That, he said, is why compasses point north. He was right.

This mattered enormously to sailors. In 1600, English, Dutch, Spanish and Portuguese ships were crossing oceans, and their navigators depended on compasses without really knowing why the needles pointed north. Some people believed that compasses were pulled by a magnetic star, or by a great magnetic mountain or island somewhere in the far north. Gilbert's terrella experiments replaced those legends with a clear, testable explanation.

Gilbert then turned to amber. To study its pull carefully he invented an instrument called the versorium, from a Latin word meaning to turn around. It was simply a light metal needle balanced on a point, a bit like a compass needle but not magnetised. When he brought a rubbed object near it, the needle swung toward the object. This made the versorium the first electroscope, a tool for detecting electric charge.

With his versorium Gilbert tested dozens of materials. He discovered that amber was not special at all. Glass, sulphur, sealing wax, resin and many gemstones, such as diamond and sapphire, also attracted light things after rubbing. Metals, on the other hand, did not seem to. He noticed that the effect worked best in dry, cold weather and faded in damp air or near a flame. And he found a key difference from magnetism: a magnet pulled only on iron, but a rubbed piece of amber or glass pulled on almost anything light, from straw to scraps of metal to drops of water.

To name this group of attracting materials, Gilbert invented the Latin word electricus, meaning like amber, from the Greek elektron. He called the substances electrics. Gilbert thought electricity and magnetism were completely separate forces. Later scientists would show they are deeply connected, but separating them was a vital first step. A few decades later, in 1646, the English writer Sir Thomas Browne used the English word electricity in print, and it soon caught on.

Gilbert died in London in 1603, the same year as Queen Elizabeth, possibly from the plague. He never lived to see what his electrics would become. But the unit of magnetomotive force, the gilbert, is named in his honour.

sections.heading: The Mayor and His Spinning Sulphur Ball
paragraphs: Rubbing amber by hand only makes a tiny amount of charge. To study electricity properly, scientists needed a way to make lots of it. The first person to build a machine for the job was a German engineer, scientist and politician named Otto von Guericke.

Guericke was the mayor of the city of Magdeburg from 1646 to 1678, at a time when the city was rebuilding after being destroyed during the Thirty Years' War. He is most famous for his experiments with air pressure. He pumped the air out of two large copper half-spheres, the Magdeburg hemispheres, fitted together, and showed that teams of horses pulling in opposite directions could not tear them apart, because the air outside pressed them together so hard.

Guericke was also curious about why things attract each other, and in the early 1660s he built a remarkable device. He made a ball of sulphur, a yellow, brittle mineral and mounted it on an iron rod so that it could be turned. As the ball spun, he rubbed it with his dry hand. The sulphur became strongly charged, far more than a rubbed lump of amber.

Guericke found that the charged ball pulled in feathers, bits of paper and other light objects, and that sometimes, after touching the ball, they were pushed away again. He had glimpsed repulsion as well as attraction, an important clue that would puzzle scientists for decades. He described his experiments in his book Experimenta Nova, published in 1672. Interestingly, Guericke did not think of his globe mainly as an electrical machine. He was using it to imitate the forces he believed held the Earth and the heavens together. Still, it is often called the first electrostatic generator, a machine for building up static electricity.

Others soon improved the idea. Around 1705 the English instrument-maker Francis Hauksbee, who worked for the Royal Society in London, spun a glass globe with the air pumped out of it. When he rubbed it, the inside of the globe glowed with an eerie purple light. Without knowing it, Hauksbee had made a distant ancestor of neon signs and fluorescent tubes. Later in the 1700s, friction machines with spinning glass globes, cylinders or plates, rubbed by leather pads, became standard equipment in every serious laboratory and many fashionable drawing rooms.

sections.heading: Stephen Gray Sends Electricity on a Journey
paragraphs: The next big step came not from a professor but from a cloth dyer. Stephen Gray was born in 1666 in Canterbury, in Kent, and trained in his family's dyeing trade. But he loved science. He taught himself astronomy, ground his own lenses, built his own telescope, and helped John Flamsteed, the first Astronomer Royal, with observations of the stars. In his old age he was poor and lived as a pensioner at the Charterhouse in London, a charity home for elderly men.

In 1729 Gray was experimenting with a long glass tube, which he charged by rubbing it. To keep dust out, he had put corks in the ends. To his surprise, he found that the corks also attracted feathers, even though he had not rubbed them. The electricity, or 'electric virtue' as people then said, had travelled from the glass into the cork. Gray wondered how far it could go. He pushed a stick into the cork, then hung an ivory ball on the end of the stick, and the ball attracted feathers too. Then he tried longer and longer pieces of string.

His rooms soon became too small, so Gray took his experiments to the country house of a friend, Granville Wheler, in Kent. There they hung a long packthread, a strong twine, across rooms and along galleries and out into the grounds. At first the experiment failed when they held the thread up with other pieces of string: the electricity escaped through the supports. Then they tried holding it up with thin threads of silk, and it worked. Charge from the rubbed glass tube travelled along the line and made a ball at the far end attract brass leaf and feathers. In the end they sent it along about 800 feet of thread, roughly 240 metres, longer than two football pitches.

Gray had discovered two kinds of materials. Some, like metal wire, damp thread and the human body, let electricity flow along them. Others, like silk, glass, resin and hair, stopped it. Today we call these conductors and insulators. A conductor is a material electricity flows through easily, like copper. An insulator blocks it, like rubber, glass or plastic. Every electric cable in your home works on Gray's discovery: a copper conductor inside, wrapped in a plastic insulator to keep the electricity where it belongs.

Gray made other clever discoveries. He found that a charged object could make a nearby object electric without even touching it, an effect now called electrostatic induction. He also compared a solid cube of oak with a hollow one of the same size and found that both carried electricity equally well. That suggested electric charge sits on the outside surface of an object rather than soaking all the way through it, an idea later scientists confirmed.

Gray's most famous demonstration became a sensation. A boy was hung horizontally in the air on silk cords, like a human hammock. A charged glass tube was brought near his feet, and suddenly his hands and face could attract scraps of paper, chaff and brass leaf from a table below. The 'flying boy' showed that the human body could carry electricity, and that the silk cords kept it from escaping to the ground. Versions of the trick were repeated in lecture halls across Europe for decades.

The Royal Society awarded Gray its Copley Medal in 1731 and again in 1732, and in 1732 welcomed him as an honorary member. Yet he remained poor, and when he died in 1736 he was probably buried in a section of a London cemetery set aside for the poor, in a spot no one can now point to. Few people today know his name, but every wire in the world carries a little bit of his legacy.

sections.heading: Du Fay Finds Two Kinds of Electricity
paragraphs: Across the English Channel, a French scientist read about Gray's experiments with excitement. Charles François de Cisternay du Fay was a chemist and member of the French Academy of Sciences, and from 1732 he was also in charge of the Jardin du Roi, the royal botanical garden in Paris. Starting in 1732 he repeated Gray's work and then went further.

Du Fay showed that almost anything could be electrified if it was kept insulated, including metals, liquids and living animals. Metals had seemed not to work only because their charge leaked straight away through the experimenter's hand. He also proved wrong an idea that the colour of an object mattered.

Then he made his most important discovery. He charged a glass tube and used it to make a tiny flake of gold leaf float away, because the gold leaf, now charged by the glass, was pushed away from it. He expected that a rubbed piece of resin would push the gold leaf away too. Instead, the resin pulled it in. Somehow the gold leaf charged by glass was attracted by charged resin. After many more tests, du Fay announced in 1733 that there were two different kinds of electricity. He called them vitreous, from the Latin word for glass, and resinous, from resin.

His rule was simple and powerful: objects with the same kind of electricity push each other apart, and objects with different kinds pull together. Two vitreous objects repel. Two resinous objects repel. A vitreous object and a resinous object attract. Du Fay imagined electricity as two invisible fluids. His paper reached English readers in 1734 through the Royal Society's journal, Philosophical Transactions.

We still use du Fay's rule today, but with different names. About fifteen years later, the American Benjamin Franklin suggested that there was really just one electric fluid, and that objects had either too much of it or too little. He called these states positive and negative. Du Fay's vitreous electricity became positive charge, and resinous electricity became negative. Today we explain it with electrons: rubbing moves tiny negatively charged electrons from one material to another, leaving one side with extra and the other short. Du Fay died of smallpox in Paris in 1739, aged about 40, but his two kinds of electricity remain at the heart of physics.

By the 1740s, electricity had become the most exciting science in Europe. Experimenters could make it with spinning machines, send it along threads, and sort it into two kinds. But it always escaped, leaking into the air or the ground within moments. They began to wonder: could electricity be caught and kept, the way you keep water in a bottle? In a town in Germany and a university city in the Netherlands, two men were about to try, using a jar of water, and one of them was about to get the nastiest surprise of his life.

deepDive: Why does rubbing make charge? The effect Gilbert studied is now called the triboelectric effect, from the Greek tribein, to rub. When two different materials touch, electrons can move from one surface to the other, because different materials hold onto their electrons with different strengths. Pull them apart and one is left with extra electrons (negative) and the other with a shortage (positive). Rubbing simply makes many more points of contact. Scientists list materials in a triboelectric series: rub glass with silk and the glass ends up positive, matching du Fay's vitreous electricity; rub amber or many resins and plastics with fur or wool and they end up negative, matching resinous electricity. Surprisingly, physicists still argue about some details, such as whether ions or tiny fragments of material also move, and why even two pieces of the same material can charge each other. Gilbert's observation that damp air spoils the effect also has a clear explanation: a thin film of water on surfaces lets charge leak away, which is why you get more static shocks in dry winter weather. Historians debate credit too. The Thales story rests on writers centuries later, so it is best treated as tradition. Gilbert separated electricity from magnetism and coined electricus, but he thought of electrics as giving off an effluvium, a kind of invisible vapour, rather than as charged. Guericke's sulphur globe is often called the first electrical machine, yet he saw it as a model of cosmic forces. Gray and Wheler's long-distance experiments are well documented in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions. Du Fay's two-fluid theory and Franklin's one-fluid theory competed for decades. In a sense both captured part of the truth: there are two kinds of charge, as du Fay said, but in metals only one kind, the electrons, actually moves, a little like Franklin's single fluid.
funFact: The strongest kind of electric eel can produce a shock of up to about 860 volts, more than three times the voltage of a British wall socket.
